_what: Glow Wild Hollow, behind Helen Edgar's Faery Yurt, down through a glowing mushroom: her ask of 2026-10-27, after Kew's 'How nature glows wild', with a jellyfish that lights up. Every sentence below is ours, and every fact names the page it was read on. tools/make-glow-wild.py writes each part's facts into glow-wild-hollow.html between glow-wild:<id> markers, and refuses a fact with no source, a Latin name, and anything about eating, picking or curing. Helen's ask of 2026-10-28 split it into three spaces she named, Air, Earth and Water, with a whirlpool down from each to the next, and a bonfire at the end under Fire.

kew.title: How nature glows wild
kew.site: Grow Wild, at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

facts.says: A living thing that makes its own light does it with a chemical reaction: a substance called luciferin meets oxygen, helped along by an enzyme called luciferase.
It is called cold light because it gives off very little heat, and it can be blue, green, yellow or red.
People have written about it for a very long time: more than two thousand years ago, Aristotle noted fungi, and the scales and eyes of fish, shining in the dark.
Much about it is still not known. A light may help something get away from whatever is hunting it, find food, or find a mate.
Most of the living things that glow live in the sea.

photos.shows: A ghost mushroom glowing pale green in the dark, in Olney State Forest, New South Wales, Australia. It is many photographs taken at different focus, stacked into one so all of it is sharp.
photos.real: Its Commons page carries the camera's record: a Fujifilm GFX100S, a 50-second exposure, 26 April 2022.

photos.shows: Small mushrooms glowing green on dark ground at night, in the Western Ghats in India.
photos.real: Its Commons page carries the camera's record: a Nikon D500, a 185-second exposure, 18 June 2026.

facts.says: Fireflies are beetles, not flies. There are more than two thousand kinds, and they are also called lightning bugs.
Most of them glow at dusk, to find a mate: some flash, and some glow steadily.
Every firefly glows when it is young, as a larva, which tells anything hunting it that it tastes bad.
Their light is cold light, yellow, green or pale red.
The glow-worm down in the earth of the hollow is a firefly too.
In Japan, parks are set aside for watching fireflies.

photos.shows: Fireflies glowing as small yellow-green lights among the trees and ferns of a forest at dusk, on Mount Paggaio in Greece.
photos.real: Its Commons page carries the camera's record: a Nikon D780, 28 June 2026.

photos.shows: Fireflies over a field of lupines at night in Maine, in a long exposure, each light a small dot or streak.
photos.real: Its Commons page carries the camera's record: a Sony NEX-5R, a 26-second exposure, 24 June 2014.

photos.shows: Fireflies drawing thin yellow-green trails through a dark garden of ferns and leaves, in a long exposure.
photos.real: Its Commons page carries the camera's record: a Nikon D800, 5 June 2017.

photos.shows: A single firefly glowing green on a leaf in the dark, in Japan.
photos.real: Its Commons page carries the camera's record: an iPhone 16, 12 June 2025.

facts.says: Moths make no light of their own, and most of them fly at night.
Moths often circle a light, and nobody is sure why. One idea is that they steer by the moon, and a light close by turns them round it in a spiral.
At night, moths carry pollen from flower to flower, including flowers that bees leave alone.

photos.shows: A pale yellow moth with its wings spread, resting on the underside of a leaf at night, in Japan.
photos.real: Its Commons page carries the camera's record: an iPhone 16, 30 May 2026.

facts.says: More than a hundred kinds of fungi are known to glow.
The glow of fungi in rotting wood is called foxfire, and also fairy fire.
Some glow mostly underground, in the fine threads they grow through soil and wood.
Nobody knows for certain why fungi glow. The light may draw in insects that carry their spores away, or warn off animals that would eat them.
Honey fungus is one of the glowing fungi that grow in the UK, though glowing fungi are rarely seen here.
Foxfire lit the compass and the barometer in the Turtle, an early submarine built in the American Revolutionary War, until cold weather stopped it glowing.

photos.shows: Small fan-shaped fungi glowing bright green on a piece of wood in the dark.
photos.real: Its Commons page carries the camera's record: a Canon EOS 5D Mark II, a 1,375-second exposure, 5 July 2010.

photos.shows: A cluster of small brown mushrooms whose stems glow green, in the Atlantic Forest in Brazil.
photos.real: Its Commons page carries the camera's record: a Canon EOS 7D Mark II, a 30-second exposure, 27 January 2020.

facts.says: Glow-worms are not worms. They are beetles.
It is the females that glow, to bring the males to them.
They live in meadows and grassland across Britain, and shine on summer nights.
In the First World War, soldiers read maps and messages by the light of glow-worms, without giving away where they were.
There are fewer glow-worms where the night is lit up by streetlights and buildings.

photos.shows: A female glow-worm holding on to a grass stem at night, the end of her body lit bright yellow-green. Photographed at Ketton Quarries in Rutland, in England.
photos.real: Its Commons page carries the camera's record: an Olympus E-M1 Mark II, a one-second exposure, 15 July 2025.

photos.shows: Half a minute of glow-worms flying low over a forest floor at night, each one drawn by the long exposure as a thin line of yellow-green light.
photos.real: Its Commons page carries the camera's record: a Nikon D850, a 30-second exposure, 1 July 2019.

photos.shows: A dark green wood at night with the light trails of flying glow-worms crossing it, in a long exposure.
photos.real: Its Commons page carries the camera's record: a Nikon D7200, an 87-second exposure, 23 June 2024.

facts.says: Fluorescence is a different thing. It is not a chemical reaction: a living thing takes in light and gives it back in a different colour.
Human eyes cannot see most natural fluorescence without ultraviolet light, though many animals can.
Mushrooms, mosses, lichens and some small animals fluoresce.

photos.shows: A mushroom seen from below under ultraviolet light, its gills and stem glowing blue, in Medellín, Colombia.
photos.real: A mycologist's photograph, kept with the record of where and when he found it on iNaturalist.

photos.shows: A small brown mushroom under ultraviolet light, its stem glowing turquoise and the underside of its cap violet.
photos.real: Its Commons page carries the camera's record: a Canon EOS 77D, a two-and-a-half-second exposure, 22 June 2025.

facts.says: Sea sparkle is a tiny living thing, a single cell, that lights up when the water around it moves.
It can be found round the coast of the UK, and has been photographed lighting up the waves at Dunraven Bay, Southerndown, in South Wales.
Fish, jellyfish and plankton in the sea make their own light too.

photos.shows: Sea sparkle lighting up blue along the wet sand and the edges of the waves on Norderney, an island off Germany's North Sea coast, as the last light goes.
photos.real: Its Commons page carries the camera's record: a Nikon D7500, a six-second exposure, 30 April 2024.

photos.shows: Waves glowing blue with sea sparkle on Yuigahama Beach in Kamakura, Japan, at night.
photos.real: Its Commons page carries the camera's record: a Nikon D5600, 5 May 2017.

photos.shows: A beach at night under clouds, with the edge of every wave glowing bright blue.
photos.real: Its Commons page carries the camera's record: a Canon EOS 5D Mark III, a two-second exposure, 26 July 2013.

photos.shows: Blue light glowing in the water along the rocky shore of the Matsu Islands, where it is called blue tears.
photos.real: Taken on 5 May 2014 and shared on Flickr then, years before pictures could be made by AI.

photos.shows: Deep-sea coral and feather stars glowing blue in the dark, on a NOAA expedition in the North Atlantic.
photos.real: Taken on a NOAA research expedition in 2009 and kept in NOAA's photo library.

facts.says: The crystal jelly lives in the Pacific Ocean off the west coast of North America, from the Bering Sea to southern California.
Its light starts out blue, made by a protein called aequorin, and a second protein in the jelly, green fluorescent protein, turns that blue into green.
Osamu Shimomura, Martin Chalfie and Roger Tsien shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their work on that green protein.
The rainbow that runs along a comb jelly is not its own light at all. It is light scattered by the rows of tiny combs it swims with.

photos.shows: A crystal jelly at the Monterey Bay Aquarium, almost clear in bright blue water, with its ring of fine canals and its long thin tentacles showing.
photos.real: Its Commons page carries the camera's record: a Sony DSC-W170, 19 January 2009.

photos.shows: A comb jelly from the deep sea, clear and lit pale blue against black.
photos.real: A marine scientist's photograph, shared on Commons in 2006, long before pictures could be made by AI.

photos.shows: A comb jelly against black, clear as glass, with rainbow colours along its rows of combs.
photos.real: A marine biologist's photograph, taken on 23 February 2013, years before pictures could be made by AI.

_photos: Every photograph is a real one, of the thing itself glowing where it could be caught glowing, and never a drawing or a picture made by AI: each says in `real` how that is known, from the camera's own record on its Commons page or from who took it and when. Each is on Wikimedia Commons under a licence this site can use, read off its own file page on 2026-10-28 (the Commons API was down that day), and was resized and saved again without camera data; nothing else was done to it. Helen's asks, 2026-10-28: real pictures like the crystals, all through the page, very clear, and no AI.

films._what: Helen's ask, 2026-10-28: films to match, from National Geographic or the like, of the forest and under the sea. Every one is on the channel of whoever made it, was checked on its own watch page (playable, allowed on other sites, its length and date), and was pressed in a frame on the live site, from the UK, and played, on 2026-10-28. The titles are theirs; the lines under them are ours.
